prompt: A classmate asks why GARCH can't be fitted by regressing volatility on its lags with least squares, the way a trend line is fitted.
why: Volatility is never observed, so there's nothing to regress on. Maximum likelihood scores parameters by how probable the observed returns are.
trap: The optimizer is how you search; the likelihood is what you search for.

prompt: In −ℓₜ = ½[ln 2π + ln σ²ₜ + e²ₜ/σ²ₜ], one term punishes a big surprise on a calm-looking day and another stops the model from predicting huge volatility every day.
tells: one term punishes a big surprise
stops the model from predicting huge volatility
why: e²/σ² penalizes surprises; ln σ² penalizes inflating σ to avoid them. Together they balance.
trap: Reading the negative log-likelihood term by term is core MLE fluency.

prompt: Multiplying the probabilities of 6,301 daily returns gives a number the computer rounds to zero, so the code adds their logarithms instead.
why: Log-likelihood turns a product into a sum and avoids underflow; the maximizer is unchanged because log is increasing.
trap: It's a numerical detail of the likelihood, not of the optimizer.

prompt: The code returns −Σ ℓₜ even though the goal is the most probable parameters.
why: Optimizers minimize, so maximizing the log-likelihood is done by minimizing its negative.

prompt: You simulate 8,000 days from a GJR-GARCH-t model with chosen settings, then fit that data blind to see whether the estimates come back close to the truth.
why: A parameter-recovery test checks that the likelihood and estimation procedure actually work.
trap: It isn't out-of-sample evaluation: the data are synthetic and the truth is known.

prompt: Near the best fit, the log-likelihood barely changes as ν moves from 6 to 10, while it drops sharply if β moves by 0.01.
why: The curvature of the log-likelihood measures precision: flat means ν is estimated loosely, sharp means β is pinned down.
trap: Standard errors come from that curvature (the inverse Hessian).
